title: Electrochemical Reduction of CO2 at Cu Nanocluster / (1010) ZnO Electrodes
abstract: The electrochemical reduction of CO2 in aqueous bicarbonate electrolytes is studied using Cu nanoclusters on single crystal 1010 ZnO electrodes. Cu is known to generate methane as a primary product in electrochemical reduction reactions while the combination of Cu and ZnO produces methanol in gas-phase synthesis reactions. In reduction experiments at −1.4 V versus Ag/AgCl, gas phase products include hydrogen, carbon monoxide, methane and ethylene and liquid phase products include methanol, ethanol, formate, methyl formate and trace levels of propanol. faradaic efficiencies of Cu/ZnO electrodes are similar relative to Cu electrodes with the exception of alcohols where selectivity is improved by an order or magnitude. In-situ FTIR analysis shows several liquid-phase products along with methoxy and formate adsorbates. The nature of the improved alcohol selectivity and intermediates are considered relative to proposed mechanisms and results from this work. © 2013 The Electrochemical Society. [DOI: 10.1149/2.105311jes] All rights reserved.

Electrochemical CO2 reduction has the potential to generate energy-dense fuels from water and atmospheric CO2 (or industrial CO2 sources) in a carbon-neutral system. Although the formal potential for CO2 reduction is near the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), several works have shown CO as a primary reduction product using electrodes with relatively high HER overpotentials such as Ag and Au. These metals show faradaic efficiencies to CO up to 87.1% at relatively high current densities (∼5.0 mA/cm2).1 More recent CO2 reduction work with Ag electrodes in imidazolium-containing electrolytes and other studies using Au25 nanoparticle electrodes have shown further increases in faradaic efficiencies for CO (near 100%) at current densities up to 15 mA/cm2.2,3 Other metals such as Pb, In, or Sn with relatively high HER overpotentials are similarly capable of producing formate or formic acid as primary products with faradaic efficiencies up to 97.4% also at relatively high current densities.1 Most interestingly, Hori et al. and others have shown Cu electrodes are capable of producing hydrocarbons (viz. methane) as primary products with faradaic efficiencies up to 83% at current densities near 5 mA/cm2.4–6
Methane has a relatively high energy density (55.6 MJ/kg)7 and is considered a valuable fuel; however electrode stability issues due to carbon deposition remains a key concern.8–10 Likewise, liquid products such as methanol have high energy densities (15.6 MJ/liter on a volumetric basis)7 and are perhaps the most valuable reduction products since alcohols are considered versatile feedstocks and may be converted to other products or liquid fuels such as dimethyl ether. Methanol is also known to be the primary product of electrochemical CO2 reduction with several types of electrodes including GaAs, InP, Ru, and oxidized Cu;8,11–13 however, reaction yields are typically low (either due to low faradaic efficiencies or low current densities) and limited electrode stability is also a common issue.9,10,12,14–19 Similarly, photoelectrochemical CO2 reduction reactions using semiconductor electrodes such as Cu-loaded TiO2 also generate methanol as a primary product; however, quantum yields are relatively low even with intense uv illumination (<10% at 345 nm).20
The fundamental nature of product selectivity, faradaic efficiencies and stability associated with Cu electrodes has been the subject of several studies.5,21–23 Hori et al. suggests that CO2 is reduced on Cu surfaces to methane occurs via a series of reactions including CO, C, and C-OH intermediates. In particular, C-OH intermediates were considered to be reduced by H2+ generated from the Heyrovsky reaction.4 Another series of recent DFT studies24–26 by Peterson et al. show the electrochemical route includes CO, HCO, H2CO and H3CO as sequential intermediates for methane formation on Cu(211) electrodes. The DFT studies suggested methane is favored over methanol

on Cu due to the preferred protonation (solution phase) of the C atom of methoxy adsorbates.24,27 Related work by Schouten et al., using online electrochemical mass spectrometry proposes the formation of methane via direct formyl (HCO) deoxygenation to a CH2 species and ultimately methane.22 In a recent electrokinetic study including water,28 Nie et al. proposes two possible reduction pathways for CO2 reduction depending on the reduction reaction of a CO intermediate. The first path involves the formation COH and leads to methane and the second involves the formation of CHO and leads to methanol. Both pathways are kinetically feasible; however, the methane pathway was found to be preferable on Cu (211) electrodes.
In this work, we consider the role of a semiconducting ZnO support on product selectivity in the reduction reaction. The combination of Cu and ZnO is well known and used commercially for gas-phase methanol synthesis from syngas mixtures. In the gas-phase reaction, ZnO is thought to help disperse Cu and is also known to improve CO2 absorption and reduction activity via synergistic behaviors.4,11,16,29,30 Here, we present product yields and faradaic efficiencies for Cu/ZnO electrodes in comparison with parallel experiments using Cu(111) electrodes. Intermediates species were studied using an electrochemical cell with in-situ FTIR (Fourier Transform Infra-Red spectroscopy) analysis. While reflection mode FTIR is difficult with Cu electrodes (primarily due to hydrogen evolution), the relatively low hydrogen generation rates and discontinuous copper clusters on a low index support (such as ZnO) enhances IR absorption.31,32

sections.heading: Experimental
sections.text:
Electrodes were fabricated by cleaning single crystal ZnO (1010) substrates (MTI Corporation), followed by vacuum deposition of Cu. The wet cleaning sequence included rinsing in deionized water, acetone, and methanol. Following the wet clean, ZnO single crystals were sputter-cleaned using cycles of Neon-ion bombardment (5 × 10−5 Torr, 1.5 kV, 15 mA, 30 minutes) at room temperature and annealed up to 700◦C (P = 10−9 Torr). A well-defined low-energy electron diffraction (LEED) pattern was used to verify long-range surface structural order. Cu (99.999%, Alfa ltd) was thermally deposited on the clean ZnO (1010) surface at room temperature for 20s to form approximately 3 monolayers (UHV 1.0 KV, 100 mA). UPS (ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy) and XPS (X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy) analyzes following Cu evaporation showed no evidence of alloy formation (without annealing).
As shown in Figure 1, clean ZnO (1010) electrode surfaces imaged by Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM, Omicron variable temperature UHV) reveals flat terraces with a high density of step edges as shown in Figure 1a. The analysis shows a depth profile of the ZnO substrate with multiple terraces separated by approximately 280 pm in

height per layer. As described by Dulub et al., the step edges provide active sites for Cu nucleation and increase Cu-O-Zn interactions.33 As shown in Figure 1b, Cu nanoclusters cover the surface with an average cluster size of 5 nm in diameter and 0.5–1 nm in height (∼3–5 layers of Cu).
Electrochemical experiments were carried out in aqueous 0.1 M KHCO3 (Sigma Aldrich) electrolytes saturated with CO2 (Air Products, 99.999%) using either a single compartment PTFE cell for in-situ FTIR (shown in Figure 2) or a 2-compartment (fritted) glass cell for (higher volume) product analysis. The custom three-electrode singlecompartment PTFE cell included an Ag/AgCl (saturated with NaCl) reference electrode and a Pt counter electrode. The single crystal cathode (with Cu nanoclusters) was located approximately 1 mm below a transparent CaF2 window and infrared absorption behavior was monitored as potentials were applied to the working electrode. Infrared spectra were collected with a Nicolet 6700 FTIR with a MercuryCadmium-Telluride (MCT) detector cooled by liquid nitrogen. The interferograms were recorded at a resolution of 4 cm−1 and over 16 scans. Voltammetric experiments including chronoamperometric experiments used for the in-situ FTIR analysis were conducted using a Princeton Applied Research 2273 potentiostat.
In parallel experiments to determine product yields, a 56 cm3 three-electrode glass cell with anode and cathode compartments was used. The counter electrode was a Pt wire, and the reference was Ag/AgCl. The reactor included a persulfonate polymer (Nafion) membrane to separate the working and counter electrodes and prevent the re-oxidation of the products. Gas phase products were detected by GC-TCD and FID (Shimadzu, GC 2014). Liquid phase products were quantified by 1D 1H NMR (Varian 700 MHz spectrometer). As described in studies5 by Kuhl et al., the product identification was carried
out (using 10 mM DMSO as a reference peak)5 by a 2D homonuclear correlation spectroscopy (COZY) experiment to determine which proton peaks are correlated in the 1H NMR spectra.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Figure 3 shows the voltammetric behavior of the Cu/ZnO and ZnO electrodes in aqueous bicarbonate electrolytes with and without CO2. As shown in Figure 3, the initial cathodic scan using Cu/ZnO electrode shows a CO2 reduction current density similar to Cu electrodes. The small shoulder near −1.1 V versus Ag/AgCl in the first scan is associated with reduction of some oxidized copper13 formed from exposure to air prior to the experiment. Voltammetric scans performed without CO2 or using only (1010) ZnO electrodes show very low current densities; reduction current densities increase slightly with the introduction of CO2 and product analysis shows hydrogen as a primary product with minor production of formates and carbon monoxide. It is important to note that previous CO2 reduction studies using polycrystalline ZnO (sintered powder) in carbonate electrolytes showed only CO and HCOO− as products along with the partial reduction of ZnO (Zn formation) at −1.4 V versus Ag/AgCl,34 however no metallic zinc or voltammetric peaks were seen with the single crystal substrates considered here at potential positive of −1.6 V versus Ag/AgCl. The Cu nanocluster - ZnO electrodes were significantly more active toward CO2 reduction showing a normalized current density of approximately 12 mA/cm2 at −1.4 V versus Ag/AgCl, which is similar to metallic Cu electrodes. Hydrogen evolution rates increase as the potential increases cathodically beyond −1.2 V and the single crystal ZnO substrate itself is reduced at potentials negative of −1.6 V versus Ag/AgCl. Liquid product analysis using the Cu nanocluster - ZnO electrode in 1h batch experiments in the glass cell, and gas product analysis with continuous CO2 flow (−1.4 V versus Ag/AgCl) are shown in Table I along with yields from parallel experiments using single crystal Cu (111) electrodes using the same electrolyte, reactors, reaction times and potentials. In both cases, reported yield data are normalized to Cu surface areas (estimated as 0.30 mm2 based on STM analysis of the Cu/ZnO electrode).
As shown in Table I, faradaic efficiencies and current densities observed with Cu(111) electrodes at −1.4 V versus Ag/AgCl (∼−0.8 V versus RHE) are similar to previous reports.4,5 It is important to note that faradaic efficiencies are potential dependent, CH4 is seen as a primary product on Cu(111) at more naegative potentials.4 At this potential (−1.4 versus Ag/AgCl), however, hydrogen is the primary product

in both cases along with significant levels of CO, HCOO−, CH4 and C2H6. Remarkably, the relative selectivity of alcohols increases by at least one order of magnitude when Cu/ZnO electrodes are used in place of Cu(111). Faradaic efficiencies are based on product analysis using both GC and NMR and their summations are slightly less than unity due to measurement limitations. Specifically, some products such as formaldehyde (easily hydrated to methanediol)35,36 cannot be easily detected by either system.37 To better understand the reaction pathway and intermediates, a custom cell was fabricated to allow in-situ infrared analysis during the reduction reaction. Cu nanocluster - ZnO electrodes were cathodically biased at the same potential (−1.4 V versus Ag/AgCl) while simultaneously collecting infra-red spectra. In the absence of potential, the only substantial change in absorbance was associated with CO2 uptake (2380 cm−1) upon carbonating the electrolyte. CO2 saturated electrolytes were used in subsequent analyzes and background spectra were acquired immediately prior to reduction experiments.
Assignments of adsorption peaks in spectra shown in Figures 4–6 were made by analogies with experimental spectra of known compounds (in the same cell) and by comparison with published literature. Initial spectra (<120s after applied potential) appear to include
adsorbed species while the mature spectra are dominated by solution species similar to those described in Table I. With the exception of methoxy and formate species, other infra-red adsorption dynamics in the early reduction period appear to be related to rearrangement of water and carbonates near the electrode.
Figures 4 and 5 show spectra collected in the initial period after applied potential focusing on specific peaks associated with surface species. As shown in Figure 4, two peaks near 1044 and 1029 cm−1 are seen within the initial 120s of applied potential. Literature reports of C-O stretching from methoxy adsorbates on Cu and ZnO surfaces occurs near 1044 cm−1 38,39 while free methanol is observed near 1030 cm−1.39,40 In this case, the absorption associated with methoxy adsorbates is relatively constant, while free methanol peak increases over time as expected from product analysis. It is also possible the peak near 1029 cm−1 is associated with free ethanol which was also determined using NMR. Further, evaporation of methanol on the same electrode showed a strong absorbance near 1045 cm−1, consistent with methoxy adsorbates. The O-H stretching modes from methanol and ethanol also contributed to the large peak observed at ∼3600 cm−1, however, this peak is also heavily influenced by the rearrangement of water near the electrode. associated with formate in the initial reduction period. Free formate is associated with the intense broad peak at 1580 cm−1 along with two small sharp peaks at 1380 and 1350 cm−1.41 In this case, adsorbed formate is indicated by C-H stretching at 1580 cm−1 and 1601 cm−1 (bridging mode).42
Figure 6 shows a mature in-situ FTIR spectra along with spectra dynamics obtained over 5 minutes at −1.4 V versus Ag/AgCl. In these spectra, the relatively broad peaks near 3600 cm−1 and 1687 cm−1 are associated with water (OH) rearrangement in electrochemical double layer. Similarly, the peaks at 1734 cm−1 and 1462 cm−1 are related to rearrangement of carbonates.43 The broad peak centered near 2137 cm−1 is due to dissolved CO1 and is consistent with gas phase product analysis. The triplet near 2900 cm−1 is associated with the stretching of C-H bonds of multiple species. In this case, the 2958 cm−1 peak is shared with several signals such as CH stretching of bidentate formate and asymmetric CH stretching of alcohols.44,45 Likewise, the 2864 cm−1 peak is shared by symmetric CH stretching of alcohols and bridging formate on copper.46 The peak at 2902 cm−1 is likely due to the symmetric CH3 stretching mode of free ethanol.46,47
It is interesting to consider the product distributions and in-situ spectra observed here relative to proposed mechanisms and theoretical predictions. Remarkably, alcohol selectivities improve by at least 1 order of magnitude with Cu/ZnO electrodes relative to Cu(111). The nature of this relative increase is not clear; however, there are several possible mechanisms. Previous experiments with oxidized Cu electrodes or Cu(I) films have shown methanol production in short experiments prior to (or along with) reduction of oxidized Cu; however, the alcohol yields observed in this case are stable and independent of reaction times. Selectivities of alcohols and C2-products are also known to be a function of crystal surfaces and the coordination level of surface copper.48 Rough Cu surfaces, particularly electrodes formed using oxidized Cu have shown significant increases in current density and increases in alcohol yields.13,49 In this case, the normalized
current densities associated with Cu nanoclusters on ZnO surfaces and Cu(111) are similar and ethylene yields are also similar. One possibility is that the ZnO supports stable low-coordinated Cu sites that favor alcohols. Another possibility is the selectivity change is related to interactions between Cu nanoclusters and the semiconducting ZnO support. The role of ZnO and the active sites for reduction have been a subject of controversy in gas-phase methanol catalysis for some time; however, there is a general consensus that CO and CO2 hydrogenation reactions occur at different sites on the Cu/ZnO surfaces.50 The ZnO is thought to help disperse copper and enhances methanol synthesis via a “Cu-ZnO synergy” effect.29 In the gas phase reaction, CO2 hydrogenation is thought to occur at Cu0 sites, and CO hydrogenation is thought to occur at Cu+ sites or Cu sites with modified electronic structures near ZnO interfaces.51 Although the gas phase CO2 pathway involves formate and does not resemble proposed electrochemical routes (where formate is considered a dead end), the reduction of CO at Cu/ZnO surfaces is thought to proceed through a series of products including CHO, CH2O and CH3O.52 Cu+ sites (or Cuδ+) are thought to be well suited for CO reduction to methanol due to σ-donor interactions and π backbonding to increase the strength of the CO bond allowing activation of the C atom for nucleophillic attack by hydrides.30 A similar synergistic effect may occur in the electrochemical case and may contribute to the improved selectivity.
It is also possible that Cu-Zn interfaces influence the reduction pathway. A recent model of the gas-phase synthesis reaction including DFT calculations suggest the Zn plays a more direct role and that active methanol sites are located near steps at Cu surfaces with Znδ+ atoms at the stepped surfaces; these sites allow stronger binding of intermediates and results in lower energy barriers and increased activity in both CO2 and CO pathways.29 While the Cu/ZnO electrodes used here (non-annealed) showed no evidence of alloy formation, it is possible that the natural interfaces of Cu and ZnO could also lower the barriers for hydrogenation of adsorbed CO. Many Body (COMB) model for the Cu/ZnO systems suggests Cu atoms near ZnO develop a positive charge when interacting with multiple oxygen atoms on ZnO surfaces.53 The magnitude of these local interactions related to the oxide support (including oxygen vacancies) under cathodic potentials are difficult to estimate, however, Cu-Zn interfaces may effect hydrogenation behavior of key intermediates such as CO* or CH3O* adsorbates.
As described in the model for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 at Cu (111) electrodes by Nie et al.28 which includes the effects of water and kinetics, there are likely two primary reduction pathways. Both paths begin with the reduction of CO2 to CO; however, methane pathway proceeds via hydrogenation of the O atom of adsorbed CO* species while the methanol pathway proceeds via hydrogenation of the C atom. In the methane path, the C-OH species is deoxygenated and the carbon atom is subsequently hydrogenated to form methane. For methanol, a formyl (CHO*) species undergoes hydrogenation to form formaldehyde (CH2O) and methoxy (CH3O) sequentially. The relative barriers determined for CO2 reduction at Cu(111) electrodes favors the methane path by a factor of approximately 2000 (∼0.18 eV). In this case with Cu/ZnO, the relative increase in selectivity toward alcohols may be associated with an increase in formation of CHO species at the critical (selectivity controlling) CO* reduction step. As mentioned previously, increased hydrogenation of the carbon atom of adsorbed CO* may be due to the relatively stronger metal-carbon binding associated with a ZnO support or interface. Independent of the mechanism for increased hydrogenation of the carbon atom, a CHO intermediate may progress to CH2O and CH3O through subsequent hydrogenation steps.
The in situ spectroscopy presented here shows CH3O* adsorbates; however, it is difficult to associate these solely with alcohol production. Indeed it is possible that methoxy adsorbates form either methane or methanol (or ethylene and ethanol). Petersen et al. suggests that the gas-phase synthesis is produces methanol since surface hydrogen is limited to react with the oxygen atoms of methoxy adsorbates. In the liquid phase, it is possible methoxy adsorbates can react with either surface hydrogen or protons in solution and the same authors indicate a 0.18 eV preference for the protonation of the carbon atom. As shown in the model by Nie et al.,28 kinetic models suggests the upright methoxy adsorbate will most likely form methanol. This model appears consistant with the experimental results shown here as we would expect to increased methoxy adsorbates consistant with increased alcohol production. Of course, there is a need for greater experimental resolution of intermediates; however many have relatively low kinetic barriers and therefore are likely to have relatively short lifetimes and limits the usefulness traditional FTIR. Formaldehyde, in particular, is a considered a key intermediate in several pathways, but has not been experimentally verified24,28 Other aldehydes such as acetylaldheyde and propionaldehyde have been experimentally identified as minor reduction products at Cu electrodes;5 however, formaldeyde is difficult to detect since it is quickly hydrated to methanediol (t1/2 < 100 ms)35,36 which cannot be easily detected in gas chromatography37 or H NMR due to interferences with water. While these results suggest methoxy adsorbates lead primarily to methanol, it would be interesting to leverage other in-situ analysis methods (e.g. ultrafast sum-frequency spectroscopy) to follow intermediates (such as formaldehyde) and their behaviors including the role of water. Ultimately the combination of in-situ tools with simulation may provide the insights needed to further tune CO2 reduction selectivity toward alcohols.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text:
CO2 reduction products including hydrogen, carbon monoxide, methane, ethylene, formate, methanol, and ethanol were observed using both Cu electrodes and Cu nanocluster- ZnO electrodes at −1.4 V versus Ag/AgCl. While the normalized current densities were similar using either type of electrode at the same potential, selectivity toward methanol and ethanol was improved by at least an order of magnitude using the Cu/ZnO electrodes. In-situ FTIR analysis showed absorption behavior consistent with several (solution-phase) products along
with formate and methoxy adsorbates. It is not clear if the methoxy adsorbates are solely associated with alcohols since other products such as methane (and ethylene) were also observed experimentally. It is possible there are several mechanisms that lead to enhanced alcohol selectivity including reactions at Cu-Zn interfaces or charge effects arising from ZnO substrates. The ZnO may strengthen of the Cu-C bond (of CO*) via σ-donor interactions and π backbonding allowing improved hydrogenation of the carbon atom, increased methoxy generation and selectivity to alcohols. Independent of the pathway, the Cu-ZnO electrodes demonstrate a stable surface for continuous CO2 reduction and significantly increase in alcohol yields.
